notes:
I've gathered substantial material from the following sources: EnduringWord.com (David Guzik), Ellicott's Commentary, Gill's Exposition, PreceptAustin.org, Ligonier.org (Reformed), and DesiringGod.org (John Piper). Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## 1 Thessalonians 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: "Now about the times and seasons, brothers, we do not need to write to you."

- **"Times and seasons"** is a Hebraism. The first word designates time in its duration (whether a longer or shorter period); the second draws attention to the *characteristics* of the period. Paul taught the Thessalonians to discern both the measurement of time and the nature of their era (Hiebert, cited by Guzik). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Ellicott notes that "times and seasons" in the original means more precisely "day and hour." The plural points to the different periods at which people might conceive the Advent likely to come. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Paul says he has no need to write, not because the topic is unimportant, but because they had been thoroughly taught. Gill notes that to write about the *time* itself would be "trifling and unnecessary" — an idle speculation — because "of that day and hour knows no man" (Matt. 24:36). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)

### v. 2: "For you are fully aware that the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night."

- **The Day of the Lord** is a familiar Old Testament expression denoting the day when God intervenes in history to judge His enemies, deliver His people, and establish His kingdom (Hiebert, cited by Guzik). In the ultimate sense it is fulfilled when Jesus judges the earth and returns in glory. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Ellicott adds that "the Lord" here means Jesus Christ, and the day means the great day of His return to judgment. The term is drawn from the OT (Joel, Isaiah, Ezekiel) where it describes the set time God fixes for any great visitation. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **"Like a thief in the night"** — meaning unexpectedly and under cover of darkness. Gill emphasises that the comparison is to the *manner* of the thief's coming (sudden, indiscernible, when not expected), not to the thief's character. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Paul's focus is not on the timing of final events but on the *uncertainty*. Whatever view one takes on the relationship of the rapture to the resurrection, "we will not be able to date the end." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/like-a-thief-in-the-night](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/like-a-thief-in-the-night)

### v. 3: "While people are saying, 'Peace and security,' destruction will come upon them suddenly, like labor pains on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape."

- **"They"** — Ellicott says this is "quite vague and general, like the French *on*." It means the world: no Christian could say "peace and safety," for Christians are ever watching. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **"Labor pains"** suggest both inevitability and unexpectedness. Guzik cites Trapp: "1. Certainly; 2. Suddenly; 3. Irresistibly, inevitably." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Gill: The metaphor also indicates the sharpness and severity of the destruction and that the cause is from within themselves (their own sins). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **Dispensational note (PreceptAustin / Constable):** The Day of the Lord in its broad sense includes the Tribulation and the Millennium. Dr. Constable says deliverance from the judgments of the Day of the Lord (the outpouring of God's wrath in the Tribulation) is certain for Christians. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-thessalonians-5.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-thessalonians-5.html)
- **Reformed alternative (Ligonier):** Some scholars believe 1 Thessalonians 5:1–11 has the destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70) more in mind — wrath to the uttermost falling on apostate Jews (see 2:16). The Romans surrounded Jerusalem when the city was bursting with Passover celebrants who thought they had "peace and safety." This is a picture of the coming destruction of the entire wicked world. [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/answers-for-the-thessalonians](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/answers-for-the-thessalonians)

### v. 4: "But you, brothers, are not in the darkness so that this day should overtake you like a thief."

- Paul shifts dramatically from "they" to "you," emphasising the stark contrast in destiny (PreceptAustin). Believers are not in the darkness of ignorance, sin, or unregeneracy, so the Day will not surprise them like a thief catching victims off guard. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_54-5](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_54-5)
- Guzik: "In addressing their behavior, Paul first simply told the Thessalonian Christians that they should be *who they are*." They have been made sons of light; now they must live up to what God has made them. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Gill: "Not in darkness" means not in a state of unregeneracy — a state of blindness and ignorance that characterises all people by nature. These saints had been called out of darkness and delivered from its power. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- PreceptAustin emphasises the Greek negative *ou* ("absolutely not") — as believers, our position is sure in Christ, the Light of the world. However, we can still *choose* to walk in darkness because we retain the flesh. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_54-5](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_54-5)

### v. 5: "For you are all sons of the light and sons of the day; we do not belong to the night or to the darkness."

- **"Sons of…"** is a Hebraism meaning "characterised by that thing" (Morris, cited by both Guzik and Constable). Believers are characterised by light and by day — in contrast to night and darkness. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Ellicott says this is "an enthusiastic Hebrew poetical turn for intimate vital connection with anything." Persons to whom darkness is an alien thing, whose natures have a kinship for light. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Gill: They are "children of the day" of the Gospel day (vs. the night of Jewish darkness), of the day of grace (vs. the night of ignorance), and of the everlasting day of glory (being heirs of the inheritance of the saints in light). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- PreceptAustin: "Day" here is not the Day of the Lord but the realm in which believers now live as light-possessed people. The contrast is with night. No definite article precedes "day." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_54-5](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_54-5)

### v. 6: "So then, let us not sleep as the others do, but let us remain awake and sober."

- **"Sleep"** — a different Greek word than the sleep of death in 4:13. It denotes indifference to spiritual realities — moral and spiritual laxity or insensibility (Hiebert). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Guzik notes that Spurgeon, in a sermon "Awake! Awake!", illustrated the tragedy of the sleeping Christian with three pictures: a doctor with a cure asleep while a plague rages; a captain asleep as the ship sinks; a man with a pardon sleeping while a prisoner awaits execution. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **"Sober"** doesn't mean humourless but describes someone who knows the proper value of things and therefore doesn't get too excited about the things of this world. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Gill extends "sober" to the mind: the heart not overcharged with the cares of this world — "men may be inebriated with the world, as well as with wine." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Christians are to be active, not passive, in waiting. Gregory Beale draws an analogy: knowing a thief may come, we lock doors and install alarms, but we don't stay home all the time. We go on with our lives, readying ourselves without being paralysed. "We are prepared, but we have to prepare ourselves further." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/how-to-wait-for-christs-return](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/how-to-wait-for-christs-return)

### v. 7: "For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who get drunk, get drunk at night."

- Ellicott: The first clause about sleep and night has already been established; this verse seems mainly inserted to justify the sudden introduction of "be sober." He notes that even heathen Thessalonica seldom saw drunken men by daylight. Among Jews, it was proof of sobriety to say "it is but the third hour of the day" (Acts 2:15). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- The logic: if Christians are "of the day," they should not behave in ways that belong to the night — whether spiritual sleep (indifference) or spiritual drunkenness (loss of self-control). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)

### v. 8: "But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation."

- Paul shifts to military imagery. A soldier is a prime example of someone who must watch and be sober, and he is equipped with armour. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- The armour here differs from Ephesians 6, indicating Paul saw the idea as a helpful picture, not something rigid (Guzik). Ellicott notes that in Ephesians the breastplate is righteousness, faith is the shield, and love disappears — here faith and love form the breastplate protecting the vital organs, and hope is the helmet protecting the head. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Gill elaborates: faith is a considerable part of the breastplate because it preserves the vitals of religion, keeps all warm and comfortable within, and secures peace and joy. Love to God and Christ keeps the believer sound in faith and practice. The helmet of hope covers the head in the day of battle and preserves from being overcome by sin and Satan. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- The Christian soldier here is defensive, not aggressive (as in Ephesians 6) — protected in breast and head against sudden blows (Ellicott). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)

### v. 9: "For God has not appointed us to suffer wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ."

- This is a foundational statement of assurance. Negatively, no wrath. Positively, obtaining salvation (future glorification). PreceptAustin calls this "vertical vision which should serve to motivate present horizontal living." [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_59-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_59-11)
- **"Appointed"** (*tithemi*) — in the middle voice, meaning God acted in His own interest; in the aorist tense, indicating this occurred in the past as a completed event (PreceptAustin). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_59-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_59-11)
- Ellicott: "Hath not appointed" — rather, "did not appoint," referring to the mysterious moment of God's eternal counsels when He fixed His predestination of us. The "wrath" is that which is to come at the Second Advent. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **"Obtain"** — Ellicott notes the Greek means more than "obtain"; it means "acquire by one's own efforts," "earn and make our own." God does not predestine to salvation without laborious acquisition on the believer's part. Yet the believer can only so acquire salvation "through our Lord Jesus Christ." Guzik agrees: "appoint" emphasises God's sovereignty but "obtain" emphasises human effort — together they show the full scope involves both divine initiative and human response. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **MacArthur (Baptist):** Paul assured them they would face "neither temporal wrath on the Day of the Lord, nor eternal wrath in hell" (cited by PreceptAustin). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_59-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_59-11)
- **Dispensational (PreceptAustin / Constable):** If the Day of the Lord commences at the midpoint of Daniel's 70th week with the bowl judgments, the wrath in view is that described in Revelation. This supports a *pre-tribulation rapture* position — the church is delivered from the wrath to come (1Th 1:10). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_59-11](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_59-11)

### v. 10: "He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him."

- **"Wake or sleep"** — here referring to life and death (not the spiritual sleep of v. 6). The Greek words differ from those used in chapter 4, but the meaning has shifted back to the topic of the dead in relation to Christ's coming. Whether believers are alive or have died, all will live together with Christ. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Guzik: "Jesus' death isn't softened by calling it sleep, but our death can be called sleep. His death *was* death, so that ours would only be sleep." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Gill: Christ died for the elect as a substitute — not merely as a martyr or example, but in the room and stead of His people as a sacrifice for their sins. The end of His dying was that they might live eternally with Him. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Ellicott: There is a sharp contrast — "who died for us" vs. "we should live." Christ's dying destroyed the power of death (Heb. 2:14); henceforth death is only a matter of being awake or asleep. "Those who sleep quite as truly live, and live with Him, as we who wake." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)

### v. 11: "Therefore encourage and build one another up, just as you are already doing."

- Paul returns to the thought of 4:18. The Thessalonians are to comfort one another about their communion with the dead who live in Christ, and to "build one another up" in settled purposes of holy living. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Guzik emphasises that Paul tells us not to *take* comfort but to *give* comfort. If all Christians have a heart to comfort each other, all will be comforted. "The idea is of a church full of active participants, not passive spectators" (Hiebert). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)

---

### vv. 12–13: Leaders in the Church
**"But we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who preside over you in the Lord and give you instruction. In love, hold them in highest regard because of their work. Live in peace with one another."**

- Three participles united under one article describe *one class of men discharging a threefold function* (Hiebert): (1) **labouring** among you, (2) **presiding** over you in the Lord (ruling, providing headship as a shepherd), (3) **admonishing** you (cautioning or reproving gently — "big-brotherly," says Morris). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Ellicott: "To know them" — the Greek indicates appreciation; they are to acquaint themselves thoroughly with the presbyter and his work, to value his example. This is the primitive idea of the priest: not a sacerdotal caste ministering to an outer world, but a superior officer in a spiritual society consisting of nothing but priests. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **Calvin (Reformed):** "In the first place he states that they *labour*. It follows from this that all idle bellies are excluded from the number of pastors." (Cited by Guzik.) [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **"Very highly in love"** — the Greek carries "such an emphasis as cannot well be expressed in English, importing esteem and love to a hyperbole" (Poole, cited by Guzik). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)

### v. 14: "And we urge you, brothers, to admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone."

- **"Unruly"** — a military word describing the soldier who breaks ranks. The self-willed person who demands to hold his own opinion. These must be warned/admonished. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **"Fainthearted"** — literally "small-souled." Those timid by nature or experience who lack courage. They need encouragement (literally, assisting strength brought to them). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **"Weak"** — those not yet ripe enough to stand firm (Ellicott). They must be upheld with an eye to building their own strength. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **John Piper (Reformed Baptist):** These three groups represent a continuum: the unruly are dysfunctional in their strength; the fainthearted are dysfunctional because of being disheartened; the weak are dysfunctional because they are physically or mentally broken. Different approaches are prescribed: admonition, encouragement, help — but all with patience. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/reflections-on-1-thessalonians-5-14-18-in-relation-to-carl-holmgren](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/reflections-on-1-thessalonians-5-14-18-in-relation-to-carl-holmgren)

### v. 15: "Make sure that no one repays evil for evil. Always pursue what is good for one another and for all people."

- Abstinence from revenge was practically a new thought for Greeks, among whom feuds were frequent and undying (Ellicott). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Guzik: The Christian never should seek revenge or vengeance, but let God take up our side. There is "not one standard of morals towards the brethren and another towards the world." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)

### v. 16: "Rejoice at all times."

- Not only in happy things but in sorrows also — because Christian joy isn't based in circumstances but in God. Circumstances change; God doesn't. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **Spurgeon:** "I have known many deeply spiritual Christian people who have been afraid to rejoice… Some take such a view of religion that it is to them a sacred duty to be gloomy." He adds, "Turn this book over and see if there be any precept that the Lord has given you in which he has said, 'Groan in the Lord always, and again I say groan.' You may groan if you like… but, at the same time, do believe that you have larger liberty to rejoice." (Cited by Guzik.) [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Ellicott: "The Christian who remains in sadness and depression really breaks a commandment: in some direction or other he mistrusts God — His power, providence, forgiveness." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)

### v. 17: "Pray without ceasing."

- Prayer is communication with God; we can live each minute in a constant, flowing conversation with God. This does not eliminate the special value of set-apart times of focused prayer, but it does mean all of life can be lived in a prayerful spirit. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Theophylact (cited by Ellicott): "This shows the way to 'rejoice always' — to wit, incessant prayer and eucharist, for he that has accustomed himself to hold converse with God … will evidently have unbroken joy." Though a man cannot be incessantly praying in words, the mind may be held continuously in an attitude of prayer, even in sleep (Song 5:2). [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)

### v. 18: "Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus."

- **"In everything"** — not *for* everything, but *in* everything. We recognise God's sovereign hand, not blind fate or chance. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Ellicott: "This is the will of God" encourages rather than merely commands — "Give thanks always, for God has no wish to give you cause for sorrow: His will towards you is to fill you with thankfulness." The phrase "in Christ Jesus" points to where this kind and loving will was most abundantly manifested. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **John Piper:** The phrase "in Christ Jesus" is the decisive phrase that changes everything. All these commands — admonish, encourage, help, rejoice, pray, give thanks — are "the will of God *in Christ Jesus* for you." Being "in Christ" means union with the living Christ: chosen in Him, redeemed in Him, justified in Him, seated with Him in heavenly places. This is what makes the commands possible. [https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/reflections-on-1-thessalonians-5-14-18-in-relation-to-carl-holmgren](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/reflections-on-1-thessalonians-5-14-18-in-relation-to-carl-holmgren)

### v. 19: "Do not extinguish the Spirit."

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (EnduringWord/Guzik):** We can quench the fire of the Spirit by doubt, indifference, rejection, or by the distraction of others. When people start to draw attention to themselves, it is a sure quench to the Spirit. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **Reformed (Ligonier/Calvin):** Ligonier notes it is hard to know exactly what Paul has in mind, but he is likely warning against disobeying the Holy Spirit by engaging in behaviours that are off-limits to believers. Importantly, Ligonier teaches that the gift of prophecy ended with the death of the last Apostle (Heb 1:1–4). "Today, prophecy means 'interpretation made suitable to present use.' Our only access to prophecy today is through the faithful exposition of the inscripturated Word of God." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/prophecies-and-discernment](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/prophecies-and-discernment)
- Ellicott: The "Spirit" here refers not too sharply to the Person of the Holy Ghost (who can never be extinguished) but to the fire of enthusiasm that should burst out in prayers, praises, thanksgivings, and prophecies. The gloom and depression at Thessalonica had almost extinguished this fire. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)

### v. 20: "Do not treat prophecies with contempt."

- Paul urges not to despise prophetic utterances. Guzik: "We recognize that the Lord speaks to and through His people today, and we learn to be open to His voice." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Ellicott: These were "cheering utterances of your prophets" (cf. Acts 15:32). The warning was needed, or would be soon, as shown by 2 Thessalonians 2:2. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **Tradition difference:** The continuationist (Pentecostal/Charismatic) reading sees this as an ongoing command to value the gift of prophecy in the church today. The cessationist (Reformed/Baptist) reading, per Ligonier, sees it as referring to the apostolic-era gift, now mediated through Scripture exposition — "we are not to despise this Word or its teaching." [https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/prophecies-and-discernment](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/prophecies-and-discernment)

### v. 21: "But test all things. Hold fast to what is good."

- Testing is primarily of prophetic utterances, but the principle applies broadly. The standard is God's Word and the discernment of spirit among the leaders. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Ellicott: "Prove all things" — "put everything to the test." Tests include: accordance with the original tradition (2Th 2:2), the supernatural inspirations of other prophets who sat as judges (1Co 14:29), and enlightened common sense (1Jn 4:1). The word "good" here means "genuine," "answering to the proper conception of what it purports to be." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Gill: "Prove all things that are said by the prophets… examine them according to the word of God the test and standard of truth; search the Scriptures, whether the things they say are true or not." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The right of private judgment is the characteristic and privilege of Protestantism. We ought thoroughly to examine all doctrines by the test of Scripture." But rationalism — the idea that reason as such is the judge of revelation — is not contained in these words. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/5-21.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/5-21.htm)

### v. 22: "Abstain from every form of evil."

- Ellicott argues the KJV translation "all appearance of evil" cannot stand. The most natural version is "Hold yourselves aloof from every evil kind" — i.e., every evil kind of whatever you may be testing. The word "evil" is used in the moral sense. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_thessalonians/5.htm)
- Guzik: "When the testing is made, any aspect of evil must be rejected. This includes evil that may come with a spiritual image." Christians must not entertain false prophets or false teaching. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)

---

### v. 23: "Now may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ."

- **"Sanctify"** — to set apart, to make different and distinct, breaking old associations and forming a new association. God *Himself* does this work; it is not our achievement. Guzik: "More Christians are defeated by self-reliance than by Satan's direct attack." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **"Spirit, soul, and body"** — This has generated centuries of debate. Guzik notes that some (like Watchman Nee) see this as supporting a trichotomist view (man as spirit, soul, and body — three distinct parts). Others see Paul simply using a Hebraistic way of saying "every part of you," without making a sharp theological distinction between spirit and soul. The phrase emphasises *completeness*. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **Trichotomy vs. Dichotomy:** This is a key theological difference. Trichotomists (spirit/soul/body as three distinct substances) appeal to this verse and Hebrews 4:12. Dichotomists (material/immaterial) argue that "spirit" and "soul" are used interchangeably in Scripture and that Paul's phrasing here is rhetorical — a prayer for *total* sanctification — not a psychological anatomy lecture. The traditional Reformed position tends toward dichotomy, while some Pentecostal and Holiness traditions have favoured trichotomy.
- The verse prays for preservation *until* the coming of Christ — the goal is blamelessness at the Parousia, not sinless perfection in this life but progressive sanctification with a view to that day.

### v. 24: "The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it."

- This grounds the prayer of v. 23 in God's character. Guzik: sanctification is God's work; He who began it will complete it (cf. Phil. 1:6). The confidence is not in human effort but in divine faithfulness. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- Gill: Paul's prayers for their perfect sanctification "were put up in faith, grounded upon the faithfulness of God who had called them to grace and glory." [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)

---

### vv. 25–28: Closing Requests

- **v. 25: "Brothers, pray for us as well."** — Paul, the apostle, asks for prayer. His humility and sense of dependence are notable. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **v. 26: "Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss."** — A cultural form of affectionate greeting in the early church, a sign of the family bond among believers. The kiss was "holy" — distinct from romantic or merely cultural kissing — and was given regardless of social rank. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **v. 27: "I charge you before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers."** — Paul's solemn adjuration indicates the letter was to be read publicly to the entire congregation, not just the leadership. This demonstrates the early church's practice of the public reading of apostolic letters, and Paul's concern that no one be excluded. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-5/)
- **v. 28: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you."** — Paul's "usual benediction" (Gill), but rich with meaning: everything begins and ends with grace. [https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_thessalonians/5.htm)

## Summary of Key Tradition Differences

| Issue | Traditions |
|-------|-----------|
| **Scope of "Day of the Lord"** | Dispensational (PreceptAustin, Constable): includes Tribulation + Millennium; believers raptured before wrath. Reformed (Ligonier): some see AD 70 as primary referent with eschatological fulfilment. |
| **Prophecy today (vv. 19–22)** | Continuationist (Pentecostal/Charismatic, EnduringWord): gift of prophecy continues; test but don't despise. Cessationist (Reformed/Ligonier): prophecy ended with the Apostles; "prophecy" now means faithful exposition of Scripture. |
| **Predestination & human effort (v. 9)** | Reformed (Ellicott, Gill): God "did not appoint" — emphasis on divine sovereign decree. Yet Ellicott stresses believers must "acquire" salvation through effort. Baptist (MacArthur, Gill): both temporal and eternal wrath in view. |
| **Trichotomy vs. Dichotomy (v. 23)** | Trichotomists (some Pentecostal/Holiness): spirit, soul, body are three distinct parts. Dichotomists (most Reformed/Baptist): "spirit and soul" are synonymous; Paul uses a rhetorical phrase for totality. |
| **"In Christ Jesus" (v. 18)** | Piper (Reformed Baptist): being "in Christ" is the decisive reality — union with Christ makes all the commands possible. This is the phrase "that changes everything." |
